1	---
2	context: todo_list
3	classification: supporting
4	owns: [todo_tasks]
5	neighbours: [guestbook:peer:shared-kernel]
6	processes: [P-02]
7	screens: []
8	features: []
9	---
10	
11	# To-do list
12	
13	One list of things to do, shared by everybody who opens the application. Anybody adds a task
14	of one line, ticks it done and back, corrects its text and deletes it; everybody reads the same
15	list, in the same order, with the same done marks. The list belongs to the application and not
16	to a browser: what one person changes, the next person to open the list sees.
17	
18	This context owns the task and every rule about it. It does not own the way between screens,
19	how a new environment is filled, or how a screen shows a failure (§ Neighbours, what no context
20	owns). The shapes on the wire are in [`spec/design/api.md`](../design/api.md); what is stored
21	is in [`spec/design/data-model.md`](../design/data-model.md). This document is the rules.
22	
23	**The header claims a screen and a black-box file only once they exist.** `screens` and
24	`features` name files, and a file that is not there yet is not claimed by writing its name
25	down early — the header is read, not admired.
26	
27	## Strategic classification
28	
29	**Supporting.** The list is specific to this application — one list every visitor shares,
30	with no accounts, under the same text rule and the same frame as the guestbook — so it is not
31	something to buy: a vendor's to-do product brings the accounts this system refuses
32	([`spec/invariants.md`](../invariants.md) § Deliberate non-goals) and a second place to go. It
33	is not what the application competes on either: its rules are deliberately few (one line, one
34	state, one order, no dates, priorities, owners or second list), and it earns the modelling of
35	one stored thing and the handful of rules below, not the apparatus a core domain gets
36	([`spec/design/architecture.md`](../design/architecture.md) § When a context deserves tactical
37	modelling).
38	
39	## Language
40	
41	| Term | What it means here |
42	|---|---|
43	| **To-do list** | The one list of tasks. There is exactly one, and everybody shares it. |
44	| **Task** | One line of text somebody put on the to-do list. It has a text, a state and a moment of adding, and nothing else: no author, no due date, no owner. |
45	| **Done / not done** | The one state a task has, switched both ways by a person. A new task is not done. |
46	| **Marking** | Setting a task done or not done. It records the state the person chose, never the opposite of what was stored. |
47	| **Moment of adding** | When the system stored the task. It orders the list and never changes. |
48	| **Line break** | Any of seven code points: U+000A, U+000B, U+000C, U+000D, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029. A task holds none inside its text (`BR-07`). In the guestbook the same characters are content — a message keeps its line breaks — and that difference is one reason these are two contexts. |
49	
50	A task is not an entry. It has no signature, no moment of amendment and no "edited" fact, and
51	an entry has no state. Neither word is used for the other thing.
52	
53	## Neighbours
54	
55	| Neighbour | Role | Pattern | What crosses, and what happens when they change it |
56	|---|---|---|---|
57	| **Guestbook** | `peer` | `shared-kernel` | **One rule crosses, and nothing else: how a text is trimmed and measured** — normalized to Unicode NFC, trimmed at both ends of the one written set of thirty code points, then counted in code points, in that order. Its words are written once, in [`guestbook.md`](guestbook.md) § `BR-01`, and this document references them and restates none of them. **The guestbook keeps** entries, signatures, messages, the edited fact, its bounds of 80 and 1000, its order in both directions, its search and its pieces. **This context keeps** tasks, done and not done, the bound of 200, the one-line rule and its set of line breaks, and its own order. No record on one side refers to a record on the other, neither reads the other's list, and neither screen shows the other's data. **When the text rule changes, both contexts change with it**, because both are held to it — so it changes only with both sets of rules in view. When the guestbook changes anything else, nothing here moves. **If the guestbook is removed, the text rule moves into this document first**, because this context is then its only holder; a citation of `BR-01` from here that points nowhere is what the specification gates catch if that is forgotten. |
58	
59	**Why a shared kernel rather than an upstream.** The guestbook supplies nothing this context
60	consumes at run time, and nothing it could change on its own without changing this context too.
61	The text rule is a fact about every text this system accepts rather than a fact about entries —
62	[`spec/design/api.md`](../design/api.md) § Collection read parameters says so for every bound
63	in the contract — and its words sit in the guestbook's document only because that was the one
64	context when they were written. Both sides are held to it; neither translates it.
65	
66	**What no context owns, and this one therefore does not either:**
67	
68	- **The way between the screens.** Reaching the to-do list from the guestbook and back, which
69	  screen the main address opens, and what the page for an unknown address says belong to the
70	  frame every screen renders inside ([`spec/design/ui/system-states.md`](../design/ui/system-states.md)).
71	- **How a new environment is filled.** Example tasks, when they are added and when they are
72	  not, are the environment's starting state
73	  ([`spec/design/architecture.md`](../design/architecture.md) § What a new environment starts
74	  with). They are bound by the rules below like any other task.
75	- **How a screen shows a failure.** That a change the application did not store is never shown
76	  as made, and that a list which could not be read is not an empty list, is how the screen
77	  behaves; its specification says how each looks.
78	
79	## `P-02` — keeping the to-do list
80	
81	One flow in five steps, each of which works on its own:
82	
83	1. **Adding.** A person types one line and adds it. The system stores the task, not done, and
84	   records its moment of adding. It appears first in the list without the person reloading.
85	2. **Reading.** Anybody sees every task on one list, newest first, done and not done alike, as
86	   the tasks are stored at the moment the list is read. Other people's changes appear on the
87	   next reading; nothing pushes them to an open screen. A list with no task on it is empty, not
88	   broken, and says what to do.
89	3. **Marking.** A person ticks a task done, or ticks it back to not done. The task stays where it
90	   is.
91	4. **Correcting.** A person changes a task's text. The state and the place stay as they are.
92	5. **Deleting.** A person asks to delete a task and is asked once to confirm. On confirmation the
93	   task is gone for good; without it, nothing changes.
94	
95	The one state a task has is switched freely in both directions. There is no other state, no
96	order of states to police, and nothing a task has to pass through.
97	
98	## Business rules
99	
100	### `BR-06` — a task needs text, and no more than 200 code points of it
101	
102	A task's text is held to the text rule this context shares with the guestbook (§ Neighbours):
103	normalized, trimmed at both ends, and only then measured. A text that is empty once trimmed is
104	refused, nothing is stored, and the person is told that a task needs text. A text longer than
105	200 code points once normalized and trimmed is refused the same way, and the person is told it
106	is too long.
107	
108	The order is what makes the bound honest. Two hundred and five spaces are an empty text, not a
109	text that is too long; two hundred code points with spaces around them are accepted and stored
110	without the spaces. Whitespace inside the text is content and is kept exactly as typed.
111	
112	**The 200 is this context's own number.** It shares its unit with the guestbook's bounds and
113	nothing else. The guestbook's search phrase is also bounded at 200: that is two rules sharing a
114	number, and moving one moves nothing on the other side.
115	
116	**The screen accepts exactly the texts the application accepts.** It never stops taking a text
117	the application would store — two hundred emoji are two hundred code points however the browser
118	counts them — and it never lets through a text the application would refuse.
119	
120	### `BR-07` — a task is one line
121	
122	A text that, once trimmed, still carries a line break (§ Language) is refused, nothing is
123	stored, and the person is told that a task is one line — a reason of its own, never "empty" or
124	"too long", so the person knows what to change.
125	
126	**A text that is also too long is refused as more than one line.** A text over 200 code points
127	with a line break inside it breaks `BR-06` and this rule at once, and the person is told one
128	reason for it — that a task is one line — on the screen and by the application alike. A pasted
129	line break such as U+2028 is often invisible in a one-line field, while a text's length is there
130	to be seen, so the reason the person cannot find for themselves is the one they are given;
131	`BR-06`'s "too long" is the reason for a text of one line.
132	
133	The rule reads the text after the trim. Every one of the seven characters is also in the trim
134	set, so a line break at either end is removed like a space and is not refused; only a line break
135	left inside the text is. A character that shows nothing but is not in the trim set, such as a
136	zero width space, is content — so a line break beside it is inside the text.
137	
138	**The seven are one written set that the screen and the application both read**, never each
139	language's own idea of a line break: the two languages this system is built in disagree about
140	some of them, and a pasted text would then be refused on one side and stored on the other.
141	
142	### `BR-08` — a task is born not done, and keeps its moment of adding
143	
144	Whatever a request to add a task claims, the new task is not done. A list does not start with
145	finished work nobody did. Its moment of adding is recorded when it is stored and never changes
146	afterwards — not by marking, not by correcting. Example tasks in a new environment follow this
147	rule too: one that is to be shown done is added not done and then marked.
148	
149	### `BR-09` — marking records the state the person chose
150	
151	Marking sets a task done or not done; it does not flip whatever is stored. Marking done a task
152	that is already done leaves it done, and marking not done a task that is already not done leaves
153	it not done. That is what keeps two people whose screens are out of date from undoing each
154	other: both chose done, and the task ends done.
155	
156	Marking never changes the text. Every task in the list shows whether it is done, a done task
157	looks different from a not-done one, and a done task's text stays as readable as any other text
158	on the screen — the floor it clears is the screen specification's.
159	
160	### `BR-10` — the text and the state are two things, changed separately
161	
162	Correcting a task changes its text and nothing else: never its state, never its moment of
163	adding. A done task can be corrected exactly as a not-done one can.
164	
165	**A correction is held to `BR-06` and `BR-07` exactly as an addition is.** A corrected text
166	either of them refuses changes nothing — the task keeps the text it had — and the person is told
167	why, with the reason an addition of that text would get.
168	
169	When two changes to one task meet — both sent before either is answered — **the later change to
170	the same thing wins, and a change to one thing never undoes the other**. Two corrections: the
171	text from the one applied later. Two markings: the state chosen in the one applied later. A
172	correction and a marking: both are kept, whichever was applied first. Nobody is told their
173	change was replaced (§ Deliberate non-goals).
174	
175	This has to hold under concurrency and not only in sequence. A correction that writes back the
176	whole task it read would restore the state it read and silently undo a marking made in between —
177	which passes every test that sends one change after another. No check made before the write can
178	hold it; the data model names the mechanism that does
179	([`spec/design/data-model.md`](../design/data-model.md)).
180	
181	### `BR-11` — the list has one order, and a task keeps its place
182	
183	Every task is on one list — done and not done alike, with no pages and no filter — ordered by
184	moment of adding, newest first. Two tasks with the same moment of adding come back in the same
185	relative order every time the list is read, so **the order is total**; without that, two people
186	could read two different lists from the same stored tasks.
187	
188	Marking and correcting never move a task. "Newest" means the moment of adding, never the moment
189	of the last change: a list reordered by its last change makes a task jump every time somebody
190	ticks it. The list is read in this one direction only.
191	
192	### `BR-12` — the same text twice is two tasks
193	
194	Adding a text identical to a task already on the list stores a second, separate task, and each
195	is marked, corrected and deleted on its own. There is deliberately no uniqueness rule here, so
196	nothing is asked of the store to hold one.
197	
198	The consequence is accepted rather than overlooked: an add whose answer was lost on the way back,
199	and which a person then repeats, leaves two tasks, and a person deletes the one they did not
200	mean. Nothing detects it.
201	
202	### `BR-13` — deletion is permanent, and a task that is gone stays gone
203	
204	A deleted task stops existing: no bin, no undo, no recovery. Every other task is left as it was.
205	Deleting somebody else's task is possible, because without accounts there is no such thing as
206	"my task".
207	
208	**A change aimed at a task that no longer exists changes nothing, creates nothing, and tells the
209	person the task no longer exists** — a marking, a correction and a second deletion alike. A write
210	that created the task again on finding it absent would bring back what somebody deleted, and
211	reporting success for a deletion that was not performed is what makes a person believe they
212	deleted twice.
213	
214	## Deliberate non-goals
215	
216	Named, so that an absence does not read as an oversight. The system-wide ones — no accounts, no
217	moderation, no retention policy, no mobile design — are in
218	[`spec/invariants.md`](../invariants.md) § Deliberate non-goals and are not restated here.
219	
220	- **More than one list, and anything on a task but its text and its state.** No due dates,
221	  priorities, assigned people, categories or notes.
222	- **Search, pages, filters and "clear all done".** Everything is on one list.
223	- **Reordering.** Neither by hand nor by state: a done task is not moved to the bottom or into a
224	  section of its own.
225	- **Live updates.** Other people's changes appear when the list is read again.
226	- **Telling a person that somebody else's change replaced theirs.** The later change wins
227	  (`BR-10`), silently.
228	- **Recording who added, marked or corrected a task.** There is nobody to record.
229	- **Detecting a duplicate.** The same text twice is two tasks (`BR-12`).
230	- **Undo and restore.** A deleted task is gone (`BR-13`).
231	
232	## Open questions
233	
234	- **Is there a largest number of tasks the list holds?** None is set, and with no pages every
235	  task is read at once. A ceiling is a product decision for a person to take, not one a design
236	  document may introduce.

---
context: todo_list
classification: supporting
owns: [todo_tasks]
neighbours: [guestbook:peer:shared-kernel]
processes: [P-02]
screens: []
features: []
---

# To-do list

One list of things to do, shared by everybody who opens the application. Anybody adds a task
of one line, ticks it done and back, corrects its text and deletes it; everybody reads the same
list, in the same order, with the same done marks. The list belongs to the application and not
to a browser: what one person changes, the next person to open the list sees.

This context owns the task and every rule about it. It does not own the way between screens,
how a new environment is filled, or how a screen shows a failure (§ Neighbours, what no context
owns). The shapes on the wire are in [`spec/design/api.md`](../design/api.md); what is stored
is in [`spec/design/data-model.md`](../design/data-model.md). This document is the rules.

**The header claims a screen and a black-box file only once they exist.** `screens` and
`features` name files, and a file that is not there yet is not claimed by writing its name
down early — the header is read, not admired.

## Strategic classification

**Supporting.** The list is specific to this application — one list every visitor shares,
with no accounts, under the same text rule and the same frame as the guestbook — so it is not
something to buy: a vendor's to-do product brings the accounts this system refuses
([`spec/invariants.md`](../invariants.md) § Deliberate non-goals) and a second place to go. It
is not what the application competes on either: its rules are deliberately few (one line, one
state, one order, no dates, priorities, owners or second list), and it earns the modelling of
one stored thing and the handful of rules below, not the apparatus a core domain gets
([`spec/design/architecture.md`](../design/architecture.md) § When a context deserves tactical
modelling).

## Language

| Term | What it means here |
|---|---|
| **To-do list** | The one list of tasks. There is exactly one, and everybody shares it. |
| **Task** | One line of text somebody put on the to-do list. It has a text, a state and a moment of adding, and nothing else: no author, no due date, no owner. |
| **Done / not done** | The one state a task has, switched both ways by a person. A new task is not done. |
| **Marking** | Setting a task done or not done. It records the state the person chose, never the opposite of what was stored. |
| **Moment of adding** | When the system stored the task. It orders the list and never changes. |
| **Line break** | Any of seven code points: U+000A, U+000B, U+000C, U+000D, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029. A task holds none inside its text (`BR-07`). In the guestbook the same characters are content — a message keeps its line breaks — and that difference is one reason these are two contexts. |

A task is not an entry. It has no signature, no moment of amendment and no "edited" fact, and
an entry has no state. Neither word is used for the other thing.

## Neighbours

| Neighbour | Role | Pattern | What crosses, and what happens when they change it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Guestbook** | `peer` | `shared-kernel` | **One rule crosses, and nothing else: how a text is trimmed and measured** — normalized to Unicode NFC, trimmed at both ends of the one written set of thirty code points, then counted in code points, in that order. Its words are written once, in [`guestbook.md`](guestbook.md) § `BR-01`, and this document references them and restates none of them. **The guestbook keeps** entries, signatures, messages, the edited fact, its bounds of 80 and 1000, its order in both directions, its search and its pieces. **This context keeps** tasks, done and not done, the bound of 200, the one-line rule and its set of line breaks, and its own order. No record on one side refers to a record on the other, neither reads the other's list, and neither screen shows the other's data. **When the text rule changes, both contexts change with it**, because both are held to it — so it changes only with both sets of rules in view. When the guestbook changes anything else, nothing here moves. **If the guestbook is removed, the text rule moves into this document first**, because this context is then its only holder; a citation of `BR-01` from here that points nowhere is what the specification gates catch if that is forgotten. |

**Why a shared kernel rather than an upstream.** The guestbook supplies nothing this context
consumes at run time, and nothing it could change on its own without changing this context too.
The text rule is a fact about every text this system accepts rather than a fact about entries —
[`spec/design/api.md`](../design/api.md) § Collection read parameters says so for every bound
in the contract — and its words sit in the guestbook's document only because that was the one
context when they were written. Both sides are held to it; neither translates it.

**What no context owns, and this one therefore does not either:**

- **The way between the screens.** Reaching the to-do list from the guestbook and back, which
  screen the main address opens, and what the page for an unknown address says belong to the
  frame every screen renders inside ([`spec/design/ui/system-states.md`](../design/ui/system-states.md)).
- **How a new environment is filled.** Example tasks, when they are added and when they are
  not, are the environment's starting state
  ([`spec/design/architecture.md`](../design/architecture.md) § What a new environment starts
  with). They are bound by the rules below like any other task.
- **How a screen shows a failure.** That a change the application did not store is never shown
  as made, and that a list which could not be read is not an empty list, is how the screen
  behaves; its specification says how each looks.

## `P-02` — keeping the to-do list

One flow in five steps, each of which works on its own:

1. **Adding.** A person types one line and adds it. The system stores the task, not done, and
   records its moment of adding. It appears first in the list without the person reloading.
2. **Reading.** Anybody sees every task on one list, newest first, done and not done alike, as
   the tasks are stored at the moment the list is read. Other people's changes appear on the
   next reading; nothing pushes them to an open screen. A list with no task on it is empty, not
   broken, and says what to do.
3. **Marking.** A person ticks a task done, or ticks it back to not done. The task stays where it
   is.
4. **Correcting.** A person changes a task's text. The state and the place stay as they are.
5. **Deleting.** A person asks to delete a task and is asked once to confirm. On confirmation the
   task is gone for good; without it, nothing changes.

The one state a task has is switched freely in both directions. There is no other state, no
order of states to police, and nothing a task has to pass through.

## Business rules

### `BR-06` — a task needs text, and no more than 200 code points of it

A task's text is held to the text rule this context shares with the guestbook (§ Neighbours):
normalized, trimmed at both ends, and only then measured. A text that is empty once trimmed is
refused, nothing is stored, and the person is told that a task needs text. A text longer than
200 code points once normalized and trimmed is refused the same way, and the person is told it
is too long.

The order is what makes the bound honest. Two hundred and five spaces are an empty text, not a
text that is too long; two hundred code points with spaces around them are accepted and stored
without the spaces. Whitespace inside the text is content and is kept exactly as typed.

**The 200 is this context's own number.** It shares its unit with the guestbook's bounds and
nothing else. The guestbook's search phrase is also bounded at 200: that is two rules sharing a
number, and moving one moves nothing on the other side.

**The screen accepts exactly the texts the application accepts.** It never stops taking a text
the application would store — two hundred emoji are two hundred code points however the browser
counts them — and it never lets through a text the application would refuse.

### `BR-07` — a task is one line

A text that, once trimmed, still carries a line break (§ Language) is refused, nothing is
stored, and the person is told that a task is one line — a reason of its own, never "empty" or
"too long", so the person knows what to change.

**A text that is also too long is refused as more than one line.** A text over 200 code points
with a line break inside it breaks `BR-06` and this rule at once, and the person is told one
reason for it — that a task is one line — on the screen and by the application alike. A pasted
line break such as U+2028 is often invisible in a one-line field, while a text's length is there
to be seen, so the reason the person cannot find for themselves is the one they are given;
`BR-06`'s "too long" is the reason for a text of one line.

The rule reads the text after the trim. Every one of the seven characters is also in the trim
set, so a line break at either end is removed like a space and is not refused; only a line break
left inside the text is. A character that shows nothing but is not in the trim set, such as a
zero width space, is content — so a line break beside it is inside the text.

**The seven are one written set that the screen and the application both read**, never each
language's own idea of a line break: the two languages this system is built in disagree about
some of them, and a pasted text would then be refused on one side and stored on the other.

### `BR-08` — a task is born not done, and keeps its moment of adding

finished work nobody did. Its moment of adding is recorded when it is stored and never changes
afterwards — not by marking, not by correcting. Example tasks in a new environment follow this
rule too: one that is to be shown done is added not done and then marked.

### `BR-09` — marking records the state the person chose

that is already done leaves it done, and marking not done a task that is already not done leaves
it not done. That is what keeps two people whose screens are out of date from undoing each
other: both chose done, and the task ends done.

Marking never changes the text. Every task in the list shows whether it is done, a done task
looks different from a not-done one, and a done task's text stays as readable as any other text
on the screen — the floor it clears is the screen specification's.

### `BR-10` — the text and the state are two things, changed separately

Correcting a task changes its text and nothing else: never its state, never its moment of
adding. A done task can be corrected exactly as a not-done one can.

**A correction is held to `BR-06` and `BR-07` exactly as an addition is.** A corrected text
either of them refuses changes nothing — the task keeps the text it had — and the person is told
why, with the reason an addition of that text would get.

When two changes to one task meet — both sent before either is answered — **the later change to
the same thing wins, and a change to one thing never undoes the other**. Two corrections: the
text from the one applied later. Two markings: the state chosen in the one applied later. A
correction and a marking: both are kept, whichever was applied first. Nobody is told their
change was replaced (§ Deliberate non-goals).

This has to hold under concurrency and not only in sequence. A correction that writes back the
whole task it read would restore the state it read and silently undo a marking made in between —
which passes every test that sends one change after another. No check made before the write can
hold it; the data model names the mechanism that does
([`spec/design/data-model.md`](../design/data-model.md)).

### `BR-11` — the list has one order, and a task keeps its place

Every task is on one list — done and not done alike, with no pages and no filter — ordered by
moment of adding, newest first. Two tasks with the same moment of adding come back in the same
relative order every time the list is read, so **the order is total**; without that, two people
could read two different lists from the same stored tasks.

Marking and correcting never move a task. "Newest" means the moment of adding, never the moment
of the last change: a list reordered by its last change makes a task jump every time somebody
ticks it. The list is read in this one direction only.

### `BR-12` — the same text twice is two tasks

Adding a text identical to a task already on the list stores a second, separate task, and each
is marked, corrected and deleted on its own. There is deliberately no uniqueness rule here, so
nothing is asked of the store to hold one.

The consequence is accepted rather than overlooked: an add whose answer was lost on the way back,
and which a person then repeats, leaves two tasks, and a person deletes the one they did not
mean. Nothing detects it.

### `BR-13` — deletion is permanent, and a task that is gone stays gone

A deleted task stops existing: no bin, no undo, no recovery. Every other task is left as it was.
Deleting somebody else's task is possible, because without accounts there is no such thing as
"my task".

**A change aimed at a task that no longer exists changes nothing, creates nothing, and tells the
person the task no longer exists** — a marking, a correction and a second deletion alike. A write
that created the task again on finding it absent would bring back what somebody deleted, and
reporting success for a deletion that was not performed is what makes a person believe they
deleted twice.

## Deliberate non-goals

Named, so that an absence does not read as an oversight. The system-wide ones — no accounts, no
moderation, no retention policy, no mobile design — are in
[`spec/invariants.md`](../invariants.md) § Deliberate non-goals and are not restated here.

- **More than one list, and anything on a task but its text and its state.** No due dates,
  priorities, assigned people, categories or notes.
- **Search, pages, filters and "clear all done".** Everything is on one list.
- **Reordering.** Neither by hand nor by state: a done task is not moved to the bottom or into a
  section of its own.
- **Live updates.** Other people's changes appear when the list is read again.
- **Telling a person that somebody else's change replaced theirs.** The later change wins
  (`BR-10`), silently.
- **Recording who added, marked or corrected a task.** There is nobody to record.
- **Detecting a duplicate.** The same text twice is two tasks (`BR-12`).
- **Undo and restore.** A deleted task is gone (`BR-13`).

## Open questions

- **Is there a largest number of tasks the list holds?** None is set, and with no pages every
  task is read at once. A ceiling is a product decision for a person to take, not one a design

# HTTP contract for the to-do list. WRITTEN BY HAND -- do not dump openapi.json here.
#
# Compatibility mode: BACKWARD. A path, an operation, a response code and an
# optional field may be added. Removing a field, changing a type, narrowing a
# numeric bound and changing a stable refusal code are breaking and raise the
# major version.
#
# What stands here is frozen and nothing else: ./scripts/contracts.sh checks every
# sentence of this file against the Pydantic dump, and the dump is allowed to carry
# more. That is why there is no `operationId`, no `title`, and no `422` where it is
# only FastAPI's automatic one for a parameter (DELETE) -- nobody asked about them,
# so they cannot answer.
#
# Self-contained on purpose. `Refusal`, `RefusalDetail`, `HTTPValidationError` and
# `ValidationError` are written out again below rather than referenced out of
# guestbook.yaml: the guestbook is the template's example and is deleted as a unit,
# and a `$ref` into its contract would leave this one unreadable on that day. The
# dump holds one schema of each name, so both files are held to the same definition
# by the same gate.
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: To-do list
  version: 1.0.0
  description: >-
    The rules behind these shapes are in spec/contexts/todo_list.md and the prose
    contract, field by field and sentence by sentence, in spec/design/api.md. This
    document states the field, the code and the cardinality in a form a machine can
    compare against the running application.

    A task's `text` is measured in CODE POINTS after it is normalized to NFC and
    trimmed of the written set of 30 code points (app/platform/schemas/text.py): 1 to
    200 of them, and one line -- none of the seven line breaks named in
    spec/contexts/todo_list.md § Language left inside. No `minLength` or `maxLength`
    is frozen on it, and that is deliberate: a text outside the bounds is refused with
    a stable code (x-refusals, below), not by a schema constraint, because the reason
    a person is given depends on which rule the text broke, and the one-line rule
    wins over the length.

paths:
  /api/todo-tasks:
    get:
      summary: List every task, newest first (BR-11)
      responses:
        "200":
          description: >-
            Always an envelope, never a bare array, and always the whole list: no
            parameters, no pieces, no filter. Newest `created_at` first, a tie settled
            by `id` in the same direction. An empty list is a 200 with an empty
            `items` and a `total` of 0, never a 404.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/TodoTaskList"
    post:
      summary: Add a task, not done (BR-06, BR-07, BR-08, BR-12)
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: "#/components/schemas/TodoTaskCreate"
      responses:
        "201":
          description: >-
            Exactly one task, as stored: its text normalized and trimmed, `done`
            false whatever the request claimed.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/TodoTaskRead"
        "422":
          description: >-
            Two shapes under one code, both intended: a coded refusal for a text that
            is empty, more than one line or too long (`todo_task_text_*`), and
            FastAPI's validation error for a body of the wrong shape.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                anyOf:
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/Refusal"
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/HTTPValidationError"

  /api/todo-tasks/{todo_task_id}:
    patch:
      summary: Mark a task, correct its text, or both (BR-09, BR-10)
      parameters:
        - name: todo_task_id
          in: path
          required: true
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: "#/components/schemas/TodoTaskUpdate"
      responses:
        "200":
          description: >-
            Exactly one task, as stored once this change is applied. Only the fields
            the body carried were written.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/TodoTaskRead"
        "404":
          description: >-
            The identifier is valid and no task has it. The code `todo_task_not_found`
            is in the body -- see x-refusals at the bottom of this file. Nothing is
            written and no task is created (BR-13).
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Refusal"
        "422":
          description: >-
            Two shapes under one code, both intended: a coded refusal for a body that
            sets no field (`todo_task_empty_patch`) or a text the rules refuse
            (`todo_task_text_*`), and FastAPI's validation error for a body of the
            wrong shape or an identifier that is not a UUID.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                anyOf:
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/Refusal"
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/HTTPValidationError"
    delete:
      summary: Delete a task for good (BR-13)
      parameters:
        - name: todo_task_id
          in: path
          required: true
      responses:
        "204":
          description: Deleted. No body.
        "404":
          description: >-
            Also on a second deletion of the same task -- a deletion that was not
            performed is never reported as one (BR-13).
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Refusal"

components:
  schemas:
    TodoTaskCreate:
      type: object
      required: [text]
      properties:
        # A required string and nothing more. The bounds are coded refusals, not
        # constraints -- see info.description. There is deliberately no `done`: a task
        # is born not done, and a `done` sent anyway is ignored (BR-08).
        text:
          type: string

    TodoTaskUpdate:
      type: object
      properties:
        # No `type`: both fields are optional, so Pydantic renders them as an `anyOf`
        # with `null`. What is frozen is their EXISTENCE and the fact that they are
        # optional; writing a type here would freeze a shape the dump does not have.
        text: {}
        done: {}

    TodoTaskRead:
      type: object
      required: [id, text, done, created_at]
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
          format: uuid
        text:
          type: string
        done:
          type: boolean
        created_at:
          type: string
          format: date-time

    TodoTaskList:
      type: object
      required: [items, total]
      properties:
        items:
          type: array
        total:
          type: integer
          minimum: 0

    Refusal:
      type: object
      required: [detail]
      properties:
        detail: {}

    RefusalDetail:
      type: object
      required: [code, message]
      properties:
        code:
          type: string
        message:
          type: string
        # No `type`: optional, so Pydantic renders an `anyOf` with `null`. Present only
        # on `todo_task_not_found`; a refusal about the body has nothing to put in it.
        id: {}

    # FastAPI's own validation shapes, frozen only because the two 422s above refer
    # to them: a `$ref` to a schema this document does not define is a document that
    # cannot be read on its own.
    HTTPValidationError:
      type: object
      properties:
        detail: {}

    ValidationError:
      type: object
      required: [loc, msg, type]
      properties:
        loc: {}
        msg:
          type: string
        type:
          type: string

# Stable refusal codes. They appear in NO OpenAPI document, because FastAPI does
# not look inside the body of a raised HTTPException -- and spec/design/api.md calls
# them a contract that never changes. This list is the only place that holds them:
# ./scripts/contracts.sh looks for each one as a literal in every routers/ directory
# under app/. The sentences are in spec/design/api.md § Refusals.
x-refusals:
  todo_task_not_found:
    status: 404
    when: the identifier is valid and no task has it -- a marking, a correction, or a second deletion
  todo_task_empty_patch:
    status: 422
    when: the PATCH sets neither text nor done
  todo_task_text_empty:
    status: 422
    when: the text is empty once normalized and trimmed
  todo_task_text_multiline:
    status: 422
    when: the text, once trimmed, still holds a line break -- also when it is over 200 code points
  todo_task_text_too_long:
    status: 422
    when: the text is one line and longer than 200 code points once normalized and trimmed

+with one of the three `todo_task_text_*` codes of § Refusals, never with FastAPI's list of

+## `todo_tasks`
+
+One row per task on the to-do list, the one list every visitor shares
+([`spec/contexts/todo_list.md`](../contexts/todo_list.md)). A task is a text, a state and a
+moment of adding; the table holds those three and the identifier, and nothing else. The model is
+`TodoTask`, in `app.contexts.todo_list.models.todo_task`.
+
+| Column | Type | Null | Notes |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| `id` | `Uuid` | no | primary key, `default=uuid.uuid4` — issued by the application, known **before** the write (§ Identifiers) |
+| `text` | `String(200)` | no | the task's one line, stored as the shared text rule leaves it — NFC, trimmed at both ends, 1 to 200 code points, no line break inside (`BR-06`, `BR-07`); the length is `TODO_TASK_TEXT_MAX_LENGTH`, below |
+| `done` | `Boolean` | no | the one state: `true` is done, `false` is not done. Written `false` on every insert whatever the request claims (`BR-08`), and afterwards only by a marking, which writes the state the person chose (`BR-09`). `default=False` on the model; no server default |
+| `created_at` | `DateTime(timezone=True)` | no | the moment of adding: set once, by the service from its clock, when the task is stored, and never assigned again — not by a marking, not by a correction (`BR-08`, `BR-10`). The list is ordered by it (`BR-11`) |
+
+**Relations: none.** The to-do list is not a row. There is exactly one list, so every row of
+`todo_tasks` is on it: a `todo_lists` table would hold one row for ever, and a `list_id` column
+would carry the same value in every row. No foreign key leaves this table and none arrives at it.
+It points at nothing in `guestbook_entries` and copies no value from it (`D-02`) — the two
+contexts share a rule about text, never a record
+([`spec/contexts/todo_list.md`](../contexts/todo_list.md) § Neighbours).
+
+**What is deliberately not a column:**
+
+- **No `updated_at`.** A task has no moment of amendment and no "edited" fact; those are an
+  entry's (`BR-02`). Nothing reads when a task last changed, and the list is never ordered by it:
+  "newest" is the moment of adding (`BR-11`).
+- **No `deleted_at`.** Deletion is a `DELETE` of the row, with no bin and no undo (`BR-13`), and a
+  done task stays the same row in the same place (`D-01`).
+- **No position.** The moment of adding is the only thing that orders the list; nothing reorders
+  it by hand or by state.
+- **Nobody.** No author, owner or "done by": the system records nobody
+  ([`spec/invariants.md`](../invariants.md) § Deliberate non-goals).
+
+**Why `String(200)`, when the message is `Text`.** The task's bound is a product rule like the
+message's, and it could move. The column holds it anyway, for two reasons the message does not
+have. A task is one line on a list, so its bound is nearer the signature's display constraint than
+a message's editorial one. And the column is the last layer's refusal of a value that arrives by
+a route that skipped the rule — a fixture, a script, a service that measured before it
+normalized, where two hundred decomposed letters are four hundred code points. Moving the bound
+is then a revision that widens the column as well as an edit to the constant; because the model
+declares the column from the constant, `tests/integration/test_migrations.py` turns red on the
+day the constant moves without that revision, rather than a write failing in production. A
+Postgres `varchar` counts code points (§ `guestbook_entries`), so the column and the rule measure
+the same thing.
+
+Rejected:
+
+- **`Text`, with the bound in the schemas alone, as the message has it.** Moving the bound would
+  be an edit to one file; the price is a column that stores whatever length a route that skipped
+  the rule sends it, and a table whose longest value nobody can read off the schema.
+- **`CHECK` constraints for the rest of the rule — an empty text, a line break inside.** That is
+  a second copy of the text rule, in SQL, beside the one in `app/platform/schemas/text.py`: the
+  trim set is thirty code points and the line breaks seven, and two hand-written copies of a set
+  agree only until one of them moves. The length is different in kind — one number, which the
+  model already reads from one constant and the model-against-revision comparison already
+  watches.
+
+**Why a boolean rather than a status.** `P-02` gives a task one state with two values, switched
+freely both ways, and no other; `done` says so in its type.
+
+Rejected:
+
+- **A `status` column over a set of values.** It is the shape that invites a third state the
+  rules do not have, and whatever then guarded the values — a `CHECK` or an enum type — would make
+  each new one a migration.
+- **A nullable `done_at` standing for both the state and when it changed.** Nothing asks when a
+  task was ticked, and "not done" would become an absence rather than a value.
+
+**The bound, beside the model.** `TODO_TASK_TEXT_MAX_LENGTH = 200` lives beside `TodoTask`; the
+column is declared from it and the schemas import it — one number, one place, bound on the same
+three routes as the guestbook's (§ `guestbook_entries`). The name is qualified because the number
+is the to-do list's own (`BR-06`): the guestbook's search phrase is also bounded at 200, by
+`QUERY_MAX_LENGTH`, and neither constant is ever read to prove the other. The to-do screen's copy
+is legal on the guestbook's terms exactly: `tests/fitness/test_length_constants.py` holds the two
+literals equal, and a corpus read by both sides checks the unit, because equal literals were not
+enough. The revision declares the literal `200` and never imports the constant: a released
+revision must not change when the constant later moves.

+guestbook's entries do (§ `guestbook_entries`, the rejected seeding from a revision; the filling
+itself is [`architecture.md`](architecture.md) § What a new environment starts with).
+
+### Two writers on one task
+
+`BR-10` asks that a correction and a marking of one task, sent at the same moment, both stick,
+and that two changes to the same thing end with the one applied later. No check made before the
+write can hold that, and no column is added to hold it. **The store holds it, through the shape
+of every write:**
+
+- a **correction** is one statement, `UPDATE todo_tasks SET text = :text WHERE id = :id
+  RETURNING …`, naming `text` alone;
+- a **marking** is one statement, `UPDATE todo_tasks SET done = :chosen WHERE id = :id
+  RETURNING …`, naming `done` alone and carrying the state the person chose — never
+  `SET done = NOT done`, and never a value computed from a state read earlier (`BR-09`);
+- a **deletion** is one statement, `DELETE FROM todo_tasks WHERE id = :id RETURNING id`.
+
+Whatever shape the contract gives the requests, a write names only the columns the person
+changed, each with the value the person sent: a request that carried the whole task back would
+be the write-back below, arriving from the browser instead of from the service. No row is read
+before any of these statements in the same request. Postgres takes the row's lock for each
+`UPDATE` and `DELETE`, and at `READ COMMITTED` — the isolation the session factory leaves in
+force — a statement that waited for the lock re-reads the row as the first writer committed it
+before it applies its own `SET`. So the column a statement does not name keeps what the other
+writer put there, and a column both name ends with the value of the one applied later.
+`RETURNING` hands back the row as the statement left it, both columns current.
+
+The read-then-writes it protects:
+
+- **A correction against a marking** — the write-back. Read the task, replace the text, write
+  back text *and* state; a marking that stored done between the read and the write is undone by
+  the not done the correction read. A correction that names `text` alone carries no state to
+  restore.
+- **Two markings from screens that are out of date** — the flip. Read the state, store its
+  opposite; two people who both chose done end with not done. A marking that writes the chosen
+  state has nothing read to go stale.
+- **A change against a deletion** — the return of the deleted. Read the task (it is there), the
+  deletion removes it, then write. A statement that matches no row changes nothing and creates
+  nothing, and no row returned is the "no longer exists" answer for a correction, a marking and a
+  second deletion alike (`BR-13`). The write that would bring the task back is an upsert —
+  `INSERT … ON CONFLICT`, or the ORM's `merge()`, which inserts on absence — and no path writes
+  one.
+
+**What defeats it, and nothing in the schema can refuse:** a write that names both columns with
+a value it read, a flip computed in SQL or in Python, or an isolation raised to
+`REPEATABLE READ`, where the waiting statement fails with a serialization error instead of
+re-reading. A sequential test passes all three exactly as it passes the shape above; only two
+writers interleaved on one row, the second waiting on the first's lock, tell them apart.
+
+Rejected:
+
+- **A version column checked on every write** (`… WHERE id = :id AND version = :read`). It
+  refuses the second writer instead of keeping both changes — the opposite of `BR-10` — and
+  telling a person their change lost is a named non-goal of the context. It would cost a column,
+  a refusal in the contract and a screen state, to undo what the rule chose.
+- **A locking read** (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, then the write). Correct, and one round trip and one
+  held lock longer than a statement that needs no read; it holds only while every path remembers
+  to take the lock, and the single statement has nothing to remember.
+- **The ORM's load, modify and flush.** It writes only the attributes that changed, so it too
+  names one column — but it reads the row first, and a deletion landing between that read and the
+  flush surfaces as a stale-data error ("0 rows matched") rather than as "no longer exists".
+

172	+**How two writers are interleaved (`CR-2609-823a/R-8`, `CR-2609-823a/R-9`).** A sequential test passes over a whole-row
173	+write-back, a flip and an upsert exactly as it passes over the statement shape
174	+[`data-model.md`](data-model.md) § Two writers on one task names, so every case in
175	+**tests/integration/test_todo_tasks_concurrency.py** runs two changes against one row with the
176	+second waiting on the first. A third connection opens a transaction and takes the row's lock
177	+(`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`). Change A starts on a thread of its own, through the service with its own
178	+session, and the test waits until `pg_stat_activity` shows one backend of this database waiting
179	+on a lock; change B starts, and the test waits for two. The holder commits, both changes finish,
180	+and the row is read. Postgres hands the row to its waiters in the order they queued, so A is
181	+applied first and B later — "applied later" is a fact the test arranged rather than one it hoped
182	+for. A case that sends one change after the other, or starts two threads with no lock held, is not
183	+this proof. Every wait is bounded at a few seconds and fails with its own message rather than
184	+hanging, and a case that needs a re-run to pass goes to quarantine, not to a retry
185	+(§ A test that flickers is not a gate). The rule these cases prove is held by the shape of a write,
186	+not by an index, so there is nothing here for a concurrent insert to prove: the to-do list has no
187	+uniqueness rule, on purpose (`BR-12`).

+**How two writers are interleaved (`CR-2609-823a/R-8`, `CR-2609-823a/R-9`).** A sequential test passes over a whole-row
+write-back, a flip and an upsert exactly as it passes over the statement shape
+[`data-model.md`](data-model.md) § Two writers on one task names, so every case in
+**tests/integration/test_todo_tasks_concurrency.py** runs two changes against one row with the
+second waiting on the first. A third connection opens a transaction and takes the row's lock
+(`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`). Change A starts on a thread of its own, through the service with its own
+session, and the test waits until `pg_stat_activity` shows one backend of this database waiting
+on a lock; change B starts, and the test waits for two. The holder commits, both changes finish,
+and the row is read. Postgres hands the row to its waiters in the order they queued, so A is
+applied first and B later — "applied later" is a fact the test arranged rather than one it hoped
+for. A case that sends one change after the other, or starts two threads with no lock held, is not
+this proof. Every wait is bounded at a few seconds and fails with its own message rather than
+hanging, and a case that needs a re-run to pass goes to quarantine, not to a retry
+(§ A test that flickers is not a gate). The rule these cases prove is held by the shape of a write,
+not by an index, so there is nothing here for a concurrent insert to prove: the to-do list has no
+uniqueness rule, on purpose (`BR-12`).
+
+**The witness for a task's text.** [`data-model.md`](data-model.md) calls for a data invariant of
+the to-do list's own, the counterpart of `D-04` for a task's text — NFC, trimmed at both ends,
+1 to 200 code points, no line break inside — and the convergence round writes it. Its witnesses
+are named here: `test_a_stored_text_is_normalized_one_line_and_within_the_bound_in_code_points` in
+**tests/integration/test_todo_tasks_service.py**, a round trip that only a real database can
+answer; `test_every_case_gets_the_verdict_the_corpus_states` in
+**tests/unit/test_todo_task_text_rules.py**, whose file the browser's rule test reads too, which
+answers whether the two sides agree; and the generator in the same unit file, which draws from
+the space the rule speaks about. Three kinds, because the invariant is about a value, about

+witness: the sweeps over `Base.metadata` in `tests/fitness/test_data_invariants.py` reach

8	
9	# To-do list
10	
11	The screen of the one shared to-do list. Anybody who opens it adds a task of one line, ticks it
12	done and back, corrects its text and deletes it, and reads the same list, newest first, as
13	everybody else — with no sign-in, because there is no identity here
14	([`../../contexts/todo_list.md`](../../contexts/todo_list.md) § `P-02`).
15	
16	The screen renders inside the page frame ([`system-states.md`](system-states.md)). The frame owns
17	the lockup, the navigation between the screens, the layout of the header and the not-found page;
18	this document owns what the to-do list puts into that frame. The mock-up in the front matter was
19	drafted by the process and approved as drafted by the person who asked for the change; it holds
20	the pixels, and this document is the specification ([`README.md`](README.md)).
21	
22	A requirement written `R-n` below is `CR-2609-823a/R-n`.
23	
24	## Regions
25	
26	Top to bottom, inside the page frame:
27	
28	1. **Header** — the frame's lockup and navigation, with "To-do list" marked as the screen on
29	   show, and on the right the number of tasks (R-5, R-3).
30	2. **Title and introductory sentence** — "Things to do", and one sentence on what the list is
31	   for and what using it costs (R-1).
32	3. **The add field** — one line and "Add task", in a white card (R-1, R-2).
33	4. **The list** — directly under the add field: every task, newest first, done and not done
34	   alike. In its place while it loads, rows in outline; when there is no task, the empty
35	   sentence; when it could not be read, the failure sentence and the error card (R-3, R-4,
36	   R-10).
37	5. **Footer** — one sentence about who sees this.
38	6. **The delete question** — above the screen, only while a deletion is being asked (R-7).
39	7. **Notices** — the frame's toasts, bottom right: what went through, and what did not (R-8,
40	   R-10).
41	
42	## Components and their states
43	
44	### The task count in the header
45	
46	| State | What the user sees |
47	|---|---|
48	| default | `6 tasks`, `1 task` — how many tasks the list holds, as last read |
49	| empty | `0 tasks` |
50	| loading | no number at all: none is shown before the list has been read |
51	| error | no number at all: a list that could not be read has no count |
52	
53	States omitted: hover, focus, active, disabled — it is a fact in text, not a control.
54	
55	### The add field (R-1, R-2)
56	
57	| State | What the user sees |
58	|---|---|
59	| default | a white card holding one borderless field, with the placeholder "What needs doing?", and "Add task" on its right. The field has no visible label and is named "New task" for assistive technology. It takes every character typed or pasted: nothing stops input at a length, and there is no character counter |
60	| focus | the screen's focus ring on the field; nothing moves |
61	| hover | "Add task", while it is open, lightens slightly; the field does not change |
62	| disabled | "Add task" is closed while the field holds no text, or holds a text the screen's rule refuses. Why: once the field has been left or Enter pressed, the rule's sentence stands under the field (`error`); before that, the empty field and its placeholder say what it is waiting for. Field and button are both locked while an add travels, and "Adding…" says why (`loading`) |
63	| error | the sentence for the one reason the text is refused, under the field, in the danger colour, announced as an alert, with the field marked invalid. Nothing is sent and the list does not change. It appears after the field is left or on Enter, never while typing, and goes as soon as the text passes |
64	| loading | "Adding…" on the button; the field and the button locked, the typed text still in the field; no row appears until the answer |
65	
66	States omitted: active — no pressed look of its own: a press shows as the state it starts,
67	`loading` or `error`; empty — the field's emptiness is its `default` state, and the empty list
68	is the list's own state, below.
69	
70	**The screen's rule is the service's rule, applied before sending** (`BR-06`, `BR-07`). The text
71	is normalized and trimmed exactly as the service will do it, then judged, in this order: empty,
72	then more than one line, then longer than 200 code points — so a text that is both too long and
73	more than one line gets the one-line sentence. The screen accepts exactly the texts the service
74	accepts: two hundred emoji are taken whole and "Add task" opens, two hundred and one are refused
75	as too long. A line feed or a carriage return never reaches the field, because a one-line field
76	drops them; the other five line breaks can be pasted, often invisibly, and are refused with the
77	one-line sentence.
78	
79	### The list (R-3, R-4, R-10)
80	
81	| State | What the user sees |
82	|---|---|
83	| loading | four rows in outline inside the list's card, with the height reserved and no spinner; read aloud as "Loading tasks". The add field is usable meanwhile |
84	| empty | "No tasks yet. Add the first one above." in a dashed frame where the list would be. Nothing reads as an error, and the header says `0 tasks` |
85	| default | every stored task in one white card, one row per task, the rows parted by hairlines, newest first, done and not done alike. Nothing to press to see more, however many tasks there are: the footer follows the last task. A list whose every task is done is this state, not `empty` |
86	| error | "The tasks could not be loaded." above the shared error card ([`system-states.md`](system-states.md) § Components and their states), whose title says what went wrong — "Could not reach the service" when nothing answered — with the detail it was given and "Try again". The empty sentence is not shown, the header shows no count, and the add field stays usable |
87	
88	States omitted: hover, focus, active, disabled — the list is not a control; the controls are in
89	its rows, below.
90	
91	**The list shows the tasks in the order they arrive and sorts nothing** (`BR-11`). A tick and a
92	correction never move a task.
93	
94	### A task's row (R-4, R-6, R-7, R-8, R-9, R-10)
95	
96	| State | What the user sees |
97	|---|---|
98	| default | an empty box, the task's text beside it, and the quiet text buttons "Edit" and "Delete" on the right, always visible. The text is the box's label, so pressing the text ticks the box too. A long text wraps inside the row, and an unbroken run breaks anywhere rather than widening the page |
99	| done | the box filled with the accent colour and ticked; the text struck through in the muted text colour and exactly as readable as any other text; the row stays where it was |
100	| hover | over the box and its text the pointer says they can be pressed; "Edit" turns the accent colour and "Delete" the danger colour; a locked control does not change |
101	| focus | the screen's focus ring around the box (the checkbox itself is not drawn), and around "Edit" and "Delete" |
102	| loading | a tick travelling: the box locked and still showing the state that is stored, with "Saving…" beside it. The row's "Edit" and "Delete" and every other row stay usable |
103	| editing | the text replaced, in place, by a bordered field holding the stored text, with the focus in it, and "Save" and "Cancel" under it; "Edit" reads "Editing". The box stays usable; "Delete" stays usable. At most one row is ever editing, and the list does not move |
104	| saving | "Saving…" on "Save"; the edit field, "Save" and "Cancel" locked; "Edit" locked on every row until the answer |
105	| deleting | behind the open question: "Deleting…" in place of "Delete", and "Edit" locked |
106	| disabled | "Edit" is closed on the row being edited, where it reads "Editing" because the editor is already open, and on every row while a correction travels, where the "Saving…" on the row being saved says why. "Delete" is closed only while its own deletion travels, and reads "Deleting…". The box is closed only while its own tick travels, with "Saving…" beside it |
107	| error | a correction the screen's rule refuses: the sentence under the edit field, announced as an alert, the field marked invalid, and "Save" closed until the text passes; "Cancel" brings back the stored text. A change that did not go through leaves the row showing what is stored — the box as it was, the text as it was — and a notice says why; a correction that did not go through keeps the editor open with what was typed, so it can be sent again or cancelled |
108	
109	States omitted: active — no pressed look of its own: a press shows as the state it starts;
110	empty — a row exists only for a stored task, and a stored task always has text (`BR-06`).
111	
112	**A task shows done in three ways at once** — the tick, the strike-through and the checked state
113	assistive technology reads — so colour is never the only carrier (`BR-09`). The done text is
114	`--color-muted`, which measures 7.09:1 on the card; it is never greyed with `--color-disabled` or
115	with opacity, which is the defect recorded in [`system-states.md`](system-states.md) § Tokens.
116	
117	**Editing happens in the row, one row at a time, and the words stay where they were read** —
118	the guestbook card's editing ([`guestbook.md`](guestbook.md) § The entry card), with the same
119	lock: while a correction travels, no editor opens anywhere, so the answer can only close the
120	editor that sent it. Opening "Edit" on another row closes the open editor, and what was typed
121	there is dropped. Ticking the box of a row being edited leaves the editor open with what was
122	typed. Escape does nothing in the editor: a stray key must not lose an edit. A done task is
123	corrected exactly as a not-done one, and its box stays ticked throughout (`BR-10`).
124	
125	### The delete question (R-7, R-8)
126	
127	| State | What the user sees |
128	|---|---|
129	| default | over the dimmed screen: "Delete this task?", the task's text quoted, "This cannot be undone.", then "Cancel", which has the focus, and "Delete task". The task is still on the list behind it |
130	| hover | "Cancel" takes the medium surface and ink text; "Delete task" lightens slightly |
131	| focus | the focus ring; the focus starts on "Cancel", and Tab stays inside the question in both directions |
132	| active | the shared buttons' own pressed look: each shrinks slightly while pressed |
133	| loading | "Deleting…" on "Delete task"; both buttons locked; Escape and a press on the backdrop do nothing; the focus rests on the question itself |
134	| disabled | both buttons, only while a deletion travels, and "Deleting…" says why |
135	
136	States omitted: empty — the question opens only for a task on the list, and quotes it; error — a
137	deletion that did not go through closes the question and is told by a notice (§ Interactions).
138	
139	**The question quotes the task it is about**, and the focus starts on "Cancel", so an Enter
140	pressed out of habit deletes nothing — the guestbook's delete dialog, and its focus rules, as
141	they are ([`guestbook.md`](guestbook.md) § The delete dialog).
142	
143	### Notices (R-8, R-10)
144	
145	| State | What the user sees |
146	|---|---|
147	| success | a dark notice at the bottom right, with a tick: "Task added.", "Task updated." or "Task deleted."; it goes by itself after a few seconds. A tick gets no notice: the box is its own confirmation |
148	| error | a dark notice with the error glyph, saying what was not done (§ Copy); it stays until it is dismissed with its "×". The screen under it is unchanged, so the lasting fact is on the screen and not only in the notice |
149	| hover | the "×" brightens |
150	| focus | the focus ring around the "×" |
151	
152	States omitted: active, disabled, loading, empty — a notice exists only while it has something
153	to say, carries nothing to wait for, and its one button is always usable and has no pressed look
154	of its own.
155	
156	## Copy
157	
158	English, like the rest of this repository ([`../conventions.md`](../conventions.md) § Language).
159	
160	| Key | Copy |
161	|---|---|
162	| screen title | `Things to do` |
163	| introductory sentence | `No account, no sign-in, one list for everybody. Add what needs doing and tick it off when it is done. Anyone can edit or delete any task.` |
164	| task count | `0 tasks` · `1 task` · `6 tasks` |
165	| add field placeholder | `What needs doing?` |
166	| add button | `Add task` |
167	| add button in flight | `Adding…` |

169	| list failed to load | `The tasks could not be loaded.` — above the shared error card, whose copy is [`system-states.md`](system-states.md) § Copy |

171	| row being edited | `Editing` |
172	| editor | `Save` · `Saving…` · `Cancel` |
173	| tick in flight | `Saving…` |
174	| deletion in flight | `Deleting…` — on the row and on the question |
175	| question — title | `Delete this task?` |

177	| question — consequence | `This cannot be undone.` |
178	| question — buttons | `Cancel` · `Delete task` · `Deleting…` |
